summary:
Mission Selene is a turn-based lunar outpost simulation built in Godot 4.7 where players manage a base for ten lunar revolutions (for simplicity, we have called them SELS). To succeed, players must keep oxygen, food, and water above zero while managing crew health, solar panel decay, and battery power.
The game addresses the challenge by turning real mission trade-offs into a daily resource loop. Each SEL, players play up to three cards, choosing whether to spend scarce battery reserves on producing supplies, repairing panels, exercising, activating radiation shelters during solar storms, or downlinking science data before storms trigger radio blackouts.
Real archived NASA DONKI solar flare data and LRO CRaTER radiation baselines are mapped onto a simplified 0–100 scale (1 unit = 0.07 mSv/day). Also, we used offline data and four-letter mission seeds. In this way, classrooms can compare strategies on identical scenarios without needing internet or API keys.
details:
What it does and how it works

Mission Selene is a turn-based strategy game where players run a lunar outpost for ten lunar revolutions, called SELS (named after Selene, the Greek goddess of the Moon). Each SEL follows a structured loop:

  • Start Phase: Players draw cards and play up to three actions per SEL, spending battery power to produce food and water, repair decaying solar panels, exercise to counter low gravity, or collect science points.
  • Crisis & Communication Management: During solar storms, players can spend 8 battery units to activate a Shelter, halving the storm's radiation spike for that time. Collected science takes one SEL to package and costs 4 battery units to downlink to Earth, though active solar storms cause radio blackouts that block transmissions.
  • End Sel Phase & LUMI Report: At the end of each day, solar panels decay, batteries charge or drain, life support resources tick down, and radiation and low gravity affect crew health. The in-game assistant, LUMI, summarizes daily resource changes. Players win by surviving all ten SELS with oxygen, food, and water above zero, while final scores reward remaining health, supplies, and downlinked science.


How it translates real science & creative approach

To avoid overwhelming young learners with raw telemetry while keeping engineering trade-offs authentic, we mapped real physical units onto a 0–100 scale defined in a configuration file. In the game, 1 radiation unit equals 0.07 mSv/day, making the base lunar exposure of 20 units roughly equivalent to the real 1.4 mSv/day lunar-surface reference. Real C, M, and X-class solar storms add +15, +35, and +60 radiation units for two SELS, with X-class storms also damaging solar panels by 10%. Every storm in the game is tied to a real historical NASA DONKI event, displaying its class, date, event ID, and a direct link to the source page. Our Data Panel also explicitly educates players on the difference between absorbed dose in silicon (µGy/h from LRO CRaTER) and human equivalent dose.


Benefits, classroom considerations, and intended impact

Our team designed Mission Selene specifically around the technical constraints of real classrooms:

  • Zero Runtime Dependencies: Web games that rely on live APIs or API keys often fail on restricted school networks. We built a Python data pipeline that fetches and embeds all NASA data at build time, allowing the web build to run 100% offline in any browser.
  • Deterministic Classroom Seeds: Each mission generates a four-letter seed shown in the top bar. Using the same seed guarantees the exact same card draw order and solar storm sequence, enabling teachers to run the same mission across an entire class and compare how different student strategies handle identical engineering crises.


Tools, coding languages, and software used

  • Game Engine & Logic: Godot Engine 4.7 and Zed as code editor using GDScript, exported to HTML5/Web using the Compatibility renderer with threads disabled for broad browser support.
  • Data Pipeline: Python 3.10+ script used at build time to query and curate JSON archives from NASA DONKI/CCMC (FLR, SEP, CME), NASA RadLab/OSDR (CRaTER-D1D2) and NASA APOD.
  • Assets: Photoshop and Illustrator for mockups and asset creation. Google Slides for the presentation. Bundled EmojiOne Color Emoji fonts.
  • AI Helps: Hermes, PI Coding agent, OpenCode all with ukisai/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27B-GSQ-RCO-GGUF model
